content.paragraph: For single integrals, the region over which we integrate is always an interval. But for double integrals, we want to be able to integrate a function not just over rectangles but also over regions of more general shape.

subsection.title: General Regions
subsection.paragraph: Consider a general region $$D$$ like the one illustrated in Figure 1. We suppose that $$D$$ is a bounded region, which means that $$D$$ can be enclosed in a rectangular region $$R$$ as in Figure 2. In order to integrate a function $$f$$ over $$D$$ we define a new function $$F$$ with domain $$R$$ by

subsection.paragraph: If $$F$$ is integrable over $$R$$ , then we define the double integral of $$f$$ over $$D$$ by

Definition 2 makes sense because $$R$$ is a rectangle and so $$\iint_{R}{F\left( {x,y} \right)\mathit{dA}}$$ has been previously defined in Section 15.1. The procedure that we have used is reasonable because the values of $$F\left( {x,y} \right)$$ are $$0$$ when $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ lies outside $$D$$ and so they contribute nothing to the integral. This means that it doesn’t matter what rectangle $$R$$ we use as long as it contains $$D$$ .

In the case where $$f\left( {x,y} \right) \geqslant 0$$ , we can still interpret $$\iint_{D}{f\left( {x,y} \right)\mathit{dA}}$$ as the volume of the solid that lies above $$D$$ and under the surface $$z = f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ (the graph of $$f$$ ). You can see that this is reasonable by comparing the graphs of $$f$$ and $$F$$ in Figures 3 and 4 and remembering that $$\iint_{R}{F\left( {x,y} \right)\mathit{dA}}$$ is the volume under the graph of $$F$$ .

subsection.paragraph: Figure 4 also shows that $$F$$ is likely to have discontinuities at the boundary points of $$D$$ . Nonetheless, if $$f$$ is continuous on $$D$$ and the boundary curve of $$D$$ is “well behaved”(in a sense outside the scope of this book), then it can be shown that $$\iint_{R}{F(x,y)\mathit{dA}}$$ exists and therefore $$\iint_{D}{f(x,y)\mathit{dA}}$$ exists. In particular, this is the case for the following two types of regions.
A plane region $$D$$ is said to be of type I if it lies between the graphs of two continuous functions of $$x$$ , that is,

note.title: Note
note.paragraph: For a type I region, the functions $$g_{1}$$ and $$g_{2}$$ must be continuous but they do not need to be defined by a single formula. For instance, in the third region of Figure 5, $$g_{2}$$ is a continuous piecewise defined function.

Observe that $$F\left( {x,y} \right) = 0$$ if $$y < g_{1}(x)$$ or $$y > g_{2}(x)$$ because $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ then lies outside $$D$$ . Therefore
because $$F{({x,y})} = f{({x,y})}$$ when $$g_{1}{(x)} \leqslant y \leqslant g_{2}{(x)}$$ . Thus we have the following formula that enables us to evaluate the double integral as an iterated integral.

problem.paragraph: Evaluate $$\iint_{D}{(x + 2y)\mathit{dA}}$$ , where $$D$$ is the region bounded by the parabolas $$y = 2x^{2}$$ and $$y = 1 + x^{2}$$ .

Solution The parabolas intersect when $$2x^{2} = 1 + x^{2}$$ , that is, $$x^{2} = 1$$ , so $$x = \pm 1$$ . We note that the region $$D$$ , sketched in Figure 8, is a type I region but not a type II region and we can write
Since the lower boundary is $$y = 2x^{2}$$ and the upper boundary is $$y = 1 + x^{2}$$ , Equation 3 gives

paragraph.math: $$\begin{array}{l} {\iint\limits_{D}{(x + 2y)\mathit{dA} = {\int_{- 1}^{1}{\int_{2x^{2}}^{1 + x^{2}}{(x + 2y)dydx}}}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{D}{(x + 2y)\mathit{dA}}} = {\int_{- 1}^{1}\left\lbrack {xy + y^{2}} \right\rbrack}_{y = 2x^{2}}^{y = 1 + x^{2}}dx} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{D}{(x + 2y)\mathit{dA}}} = {\int_{- 1}^{1}{\lbrack x(1 + x^{2}) + {(1 + x^{2})}^{2} - x(2x^{2}) - {(2x^{2})}^{2}\rbrack dx}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{D}{(x + 2y)\mathit{dA}}} = {\int_{- 1}^{1}{( - 3x^{4} - x^{3} + 2x^{2} + x + 1)dx}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{D}{(x + 2y)\mathit{dA}}} = \left. - 3\frac{x^{5}}{5} - \frac{x^{4}}{4} + 2\frac{x^{3}}{3} + \frac{x^{2}}{2} + x \right\rbrack_{- 1}^{1} = \frac{32}{15}} \end{array}$$

note.title: Note
note.paragraph: When we set up a double integral as in Example 1, it is essential to draw a diagram. Often it is helpful to draw a vertical arrow as in Figure 8. Then the limits of integration for the inner integral can be read from the diagram as follows: The arrow starts at the lower boundary $$y = g_{1}(x)$$ , which gives the lower limit in the integral, and the arrow ends at the upper boundary $$y = g_{2}(x)$$ , which gives the upper limit of integration. For a type II region the arrow is drawn horizontally from the left boundary to the right boundary.

subsection.title: Changing the Order of Integration
subsection.paragraph: Fubini’s Theorem tells us that we can express a double integral as an iterated integral in two different orders. Sometimes one order is much more difficult to evaluate than the other—or even impossible. The next example shows how we can change the order of integration when presented with an iterated integral that is difficult to evaluate.

problem.paragraph: Evaluate the iterated integral $$\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{x}^{1}{\sin{(y^{2})}dydx}}$$ .

Solution If we try to evaluate the integral as it stands, we are faced with the task of first evaluating $$\int{\sin{(y^{2})}dy}$$ . But it’s impossible to do so in finite terms since $$\int{\sin{(y^{2})}dy}$$ is not an elementary function. (See the end of Section 7.5.) So we must change the order of integration.
